name: ESP32-DIV v1
firmware_note: One firmware source, built per board: v1 (plain ESP32), v2 (ESP32-S3), and a build for the generic ESP32-2432S028 'Cheap Yellow Display' board.
price_note: ESTIMATE, parts only, single unit. ESP32-WROOM-32 ~$5, 2.8in ILI9341 TFT with XPT2046 touch ~$10, 3x nRF24L01+ ~$8-12 (PA/LNA versions cost more), CC1101 ~$4, IR TX/RX ~$2, CP2102 ~$2, IP5306 ~$2, PCF8574 ~$1, LF33 ~$1, microSD slot, buzzer, WS2812s, buttons and passives ~$8, LiPo cell ~$6, antennas and IPEX pigtails ~$8. The cost people forget: two PCBs (main + shield) at JLCPCB's minimum order of five each, ~$20-30 shipped, plus a printed case ~$10. A single finished unit realistically lands at $70-95 and assumes you already own a soldering station and hot air.
skill_note: Two custom PCBs with fine-pitch SMD parts plus three stacked RF modules that must be powered without browning out the ESP32 - you must be comfortable with SMD soldering, reading a schematic, and debugging a board that will not enumerate.
build_note: Gerbers are in the repo (PCB/v1). You order the boards, source about forty distinct parts, solder them, then flash from the browser at cifertech.github.io/ESP32-DIV. No kit exists and the author sells nothing assembled.
summary: A handheld open-source wireless toolkit: a plain ESP32 driving a 2.8in touchscreen, with a plug-on shield carrying three nRF24L01+ modules, a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver and an IR transceiver. Wi-Fi and BLE come from the ESP32's own radio, 2.4GHz ShockBurst and MouseJack from the nRF24s, 300-928MHz replay from the CC1101. It is a project you build, not a product you buy.
honest_take: Genuinely capable for the parts cost, but the author's own 'better than Flipper' framing is marketing. All Wi-Fi is 2.4GHz only; deauth works only against WPA2 networks that have not enabled 802.11w/PMF, and WPA3 mandates PMF so it is immune. The RFID/NFC and GPS menus in the feature list need a PN532 and a GNSS module that are not on the published BOM - you add them yourself. And if you would rather not solder two custom PCBs, the same firmware has a build for the ~$12 ESP32-2432S028 'CYD' board, which with a $15-25 RF companion hat gets you most of this for a third of the work.

wifi_scan_24.note: Scanner with extended detail; a separate WPS scanner flags WPS-enabled APs.

wifi_scan_5.note: ESP32 radio is 2.4GHz only. No 5GHz on any ESP32-DIV build.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Sends deauth management frames. Only works where 802.11w/PMF is off. WPA3 mandates PMF and modern WPA2 gear increasingly enables it, in which case this does nothing at all.

wifi_beacon_spam.note: Broadcasts custom or random fake SSIDs.

wifi_evil_twin.note: 'Captive Portal' tool: AP plus DNS hijack plus web server to clone a network and serve a sign-in page.

wifi_captive_portal.note: Same module; portal templates stored on SD.

wifi_karma.note: Listens for probe requests and impersonates the named network to attract auto-connect.

wifi_probe_sniff.note: Probe Flood transmits; the packet monitor and Karma module read probe requests.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: ESP32 promiscuous mode, not true monitor mode - you get management and control frames plus a 14-channel waterfall, with optional PCAP to SD. Not a substitute for an Atheros or Ralink card.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: PCAP logging is documented but EAPOL handshake or PMKID capture is never claimed, and could not be confirmed from the repo.

wifi_wardriving.note: Logs in WiGLE format but needs a GNSS module you add yourself - there is no GPS on the published BOM.

ble_scan.note: Scanner plus a sniffer view tracking MAC, RSSI, packet count and last-seen time.

ble_advertise.note: BLE Spoofer broadcasts arbitrary advertisements from the ESP32 radio.

ble_spam_apple.note: 'Sour Apple' floods Apple proximity-pairing advertisements to trigger popups on nearby iPhones. A nuisance, not a compromise.

ble_spam_android.note: Not named separately in the feature table; the generic BLE Spoofer could be pointed at it.

ble_hid.note: 'BLE Rubber Ducky' pairs as a BLE keyboard and runs DuckyScript from /ducky on SD. The target has to accept the pairing first.

ble_jam.note: nRF24 modules spew on the BLE advertising channels. Effective at close range against advertising and pairing; an established connection already hopping across 37 data channels is far more resilient.

ble_tracker_detect.note: AirTag Sniffer matches Apple Find My advertising payloads. Blind to a tracker that is not currently advertising.

ble_tracker_spoof.note: AirTag Spoofer broadcasts fabricated Find My advertisements.

findmy_track.note: Broadcasts into the Find My network; it does not query Apple's servers or locate anything itself.

detect_skimmer.note: A BLE scan matched against signatures of the cheap Bluetooth serial modules typical of card skimmers (default HC-05/HC-06 style names). Defeated by renaming the module, and it false-positives on innocent hobby projects.

detect_generic_wifi.note: Deauth Detector counts inbound deauth and disassoc frames on the current channel.

nrf24_scan.note: 128-channel 2.4GHz energy scan drawn as a spectrum waterfall. Energy only - it does not demodulate Zigbee or Wi-Fi.

nrf24_jam.note: 'Protokill' floods selected channels using three nRF24s. Real interference over a few metres on a few 1MHz channels at a time, not a wideband band-kill, and illegal to operate in the US and most of Europe regardless of range.

mousejack.note: Scan and keystroke injection against unencrypted 2.4GHz keyboard and mouse dongles (Bastille, 2016). Most dongles sold since about 2017 are patched, so success depends on finding old hardware.

zigbee.note: It can put energy on Zigbee channels; it cannot speak Zigbee, join a network or decode a frame.

subghz_tx.note: Same CC1101, with no region lock in firmware - the legal responsibility is entirely yours.

subghz_replay.note: Capture, store to SD as named profiles, replay.

subghz_rolling_code.note: Replaying a captured rolling code fails by design. There is no KeeLoq or rolling-code defeat here.

subghz_bruteforce.note: De Bruijn sequence generator, for fixed-code dip-switch-era remotes only.

ir_rx.note: Captures and visualises the waveform and preserves carrier frequency.

ir_universal_remote.note: Built-in profile database plus SD imports.

lf_125khz_read.note: No 125kHz analogue front end anywhere in the design.

hf_1356_read.note: The firmware has a full RFID/NFC menu (read, clone, dump, erase) but no NFC IC appears on the published main-board or shield BOM. You add a PN532 module on the expansion pins yourself.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Same user-added PN532 dependency, and emulation on a PN532 is limited to simple tag types.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: 'Dump' reads sectors only when you already hold the keys. There is no nested, darkside or hardnested key recovery.

gps.note: Satellite scanner and wardriver exist in firmware; the GNSS module is not on the BOM.

sd_logging.note: PCAP, IR, sub-GHz and wardrive logs.

scriptable.note: DuckyScript for the BLE HID module only. No general scripting or app system.

standalone_untethered.note: Battery powered with a touchscreen UI.

usb_hid_inject.note: The plain ESP32 has no USB peripheral, so HID injection is over BLE only. The v2's ESP32-S3 does have native USB.

legal.notes: Building and owning the board is generally legal; several of its headline functions are not. In the United States the FCC treats intentional jammers as illegal to market, sell or operate under 47 U.S.C. 302a and 333, with no exception for private individuals, and has applied the same reasoning to Wi-Fi deauthentication - Marriott paid a $600,000 consent decree in 2014 for deauthing guest hotspots. Transmitting on sub-GHz bands without a licence, and injecting keystrokes into someone else's wireless keyboard, are separate offences in most countries. Check your local law; this is a description, not legal advice.

ecosystem.app_store: No - monolithic firmware, no plugin or app system

summary: The second-generation ESP32-DIV: an ESP32-S3 main board with a 2.8in touchscreen, IP5306 battery management, microSD and four status NeoPixels, plus a pogo-pin stacking shield carrying three nRF24L01+ modules, a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver and an IR transceiver. honest_take: The author's blog headline is 'I built something better than Flipper', and that is the claim to be sceptical about. It has more radios than a Flipper for less money, but it is a hand-soldered two-board project with no case, no app ecosystem, no NFC or GPS unless you bolt them on, and no 5GHz - and the Flipper's value was always polish and the software catalogue, not the silicon. Buy the comparison on radios; do not buy it on usability. name: RF-Clown v1
firmware_note: Three modes - BLE, Classic Bluetooth, and combined - driving the nRF24 modules, with a NeoPixel as the only status indicator.
price_note: ESTIMATE, parts only. ESP32 module ~$5, 2x nRF24L01+ (PA/LNA versions ~$4 each, plain ~$1.50 each) ~$4-9, TP4056 charger ~$1, LF33 regulator ~$1, NeoPixel and passives ~$3, LiPo cell ~$6, antennas/pigtails ~$6. The custom PCB is the hidden cost: JLCPCB's minimum order is 5 boards, ~$12-20 shipped. A single finished unit realistically lands at $40-55. No case is provided.
skill_note: One small PCB with a handful of SMD parts and two through-hole radio modules - simpler than the ESP32-DIV, but you still need to solder, flash, and understand why two transmitting nRF24s can brown out a badly decoupled 3.3V rail.
build_note: Order the PCB from the repo's gerbers, solder the ESP32, TP4056, regulator and two nRF24 modules, then flash the Arduino firmware. Superseded by v2 - if you are starting now, build v2.
summary: The first RF-Clown: a small ESP32 board carrying two nRF24L01+ modules whose only job is to flood the 2.4GHz advertising and pairing channels used by BLE and Classic Bluetooth. There is no display - a NeoPixel tells you which of the three modes is running. It has been superseded by v2 and exists now mainly as a reference design.
honest_take: This is a jammer with an educational README, and no amount of 'for testing and learning' framing changes what it is - in the US, operating it is flatly illegal under FCC rules, with no exception for hobbyists. Technically it is also weaker than the name implies: two nRF24s can only sit on a couple of 1MHz channels at a time, so it reliably breaks BLE advertising and pairing within a few metres but does far less to an established, frequency-hopping Bluetooth link. If you want to learn 2.4GHz RF rather than break it, the nRFBox from the same author does scanning and analysis too.

Its purpose is unchanged - flooding the 2.4GHz channels that BLE and Classic Bluetooth depend on.
honest_take: More radios and 8dBi antennas make this meaningfully more disruptive than v1, and that is the problem: it is a better jammer, and jammers are illegal to operate in the US, UK and most of the EU with no hobbyist exemption. The 'testing and learning' framing in the README does not create a legal defence. Technically, be clear about what three nRF24s buy you - three simultaneous 1MHz channels of narrowband energy, not a wall of noise across the band; BLE advertising and pairing fall over quickly, established hopping links often limp on. summary: A Raspberry Pi in a small case with an e-ink screen that walks around collecting WPA handshake material. It drives bettercap to capture PMKIDs and full or half WPA handshakes into PCAPNG files for later cracking with hashcat, and shows an animated face on the display reflecting what it is doing. Multiple units in range advertise their presence to each other using custom information elements in 802.11 beacons.
honest_take: Two things people get wrong. First, the AI: the maintained fork removed it entirely - the maintainer's README says AI destabilised the Wi-Fi firmware, so it was cut for uptime and battery life. Even when present, it was reinforcement learning tuning channel-hop and dwell parameters, not anything that understood networks. Second, it does not crack anything. It collects handshake material; the actual cracking happens later on a real GPU, and if the target's password is not in your wordlist you get nothing at all. Add that most of what it captures is from networks you have no permission to touch, and the honest description is 'a Tamagotchi that generates hashcat homework'.

summary: A Raspberry Pi with a 2.13in e-ink screen that autonomously works a network: it discovers live hosts, scans ports, fingerprints services, runs Nmap vulnerability scripts, then brute-forces FTP, SSH, SMB, RDP, Telnet and SQL logins and pulls files off anything it gets into. honest_take: Be very clear what this is: it is not a passive collector like a Pwnagotchi, it is an autonomous credential brute-forcer that steals files, and running it on a network you do not own is straightforwardly a crime in most countries - the cute Viking does not change that. Technically there is nothing here you could not do with a shell script wrapping nmap and hydra; what Bjorn adds is the orchestration, the e-ink UI and the game loop. It also brute-forces loudly, so any network with account lockout, fail2ban or basic monitoring will catch it almost immediately. The 6,000+ stars measure how good the idea looks in a demo video, not how useful it is on a real engagement.

That is ~$60-70. The number people miss is the Wi-Fi adapter: the onboard Pi Wi-Fi cannot do monitor mode or injection here, so Wi-Fi attacks need an external USB adapter - an Alfa AWUS036ACH is ~$50, which nearly doubles the build. summary: An offensive network toolkit for a Raspberry Pi with a small joystick LCD HAT, styled after Hak5's Shark Jack and pager-format tools. You plug it into a LAN or attach a USB Wi-Fi adapter and drive 231 bundled payloads from the on-device joystick menu or a browser IDE: Nmap recon, ARP MITM and DNS spoofing, evil portals with 84 templates, Wi-Fi deauth and handshake hunting, Bluetooth attacks, and exfiltration over HTTP, DNS, Discord, SMB, FTP and Dropbox.
honest_take: The single most important thing to get right is the Wi-Fi adapter, and the project's own recommendation list contains a trap. The TP-Link TL-WN722N is listed as 'v1' for a reason: only the original Atheros AR9271 version does monitor mode and injection, and essentially everything sold under that name today is a v2 or v3 with a Realtek RTL8188EUS that does not. Buy the wrong one and every Wi-Fi payload silently fails. Beyond that, the 231-payload count is impressive breadth but wildly uneven depth - 25 of them are games, and the security payloads range from genuinely useful to thin wrappers around a single command. It is also very new (repo created June 2025), so expect churn.

summary: A two-chip BadUSB: an ATmega32u4 emulates a USB keyboard while an ESP8266 next to it hosts a Wi-Fi access point and web interface, so you can write, edit and fire DuckyScript payloads remotely instead of pulling the device out to reflash it. honest_take: The elephant: this project is dormant. The last code commit to the default branch was February 2022, the newest release is a release candidate from January 2022, and there are 22 open issues with nobody closing them. It still works - keystroke injection has not changed - but nothing is being fixed and no new keyboard layouts are landing, so check the layout list before you build. Also note it is genuinely just two commodity dev boards and four wires: if someone sells you a 'WiFi Duck' for $60, you are paying for a PCB and a case. And be clear about the trade-off you are making versus a plain Rubber Ducky clone: you gain remote control, and you add an ESP8266 broadcasting an access point next to the machine you are attacking.

firmware_note: A full Raspbian-based image, not an app you install. Original author MaMe82 stopped; RoganDawes took over the repo, and its last code push was October 2023.

build_note: Flash the image to a card and plug the Pi Zero W into a host over its USB data port. No soldering. Kali Linux also publishes a P4wnP1 A.L.O.A. ARM image, which is the more reliably updated route.
summary: A Raspberry Pi Zero W that turns into whatever USB device you tell it to be: HID keyboard and mouse, USB Ethernet (RNDIS and CDC ECM), mass storage, or several at once. That composite-gadget ability is what set it apart from single-purpose BadUSBs - it can type a payload and simultaneously become the target's network interface, then serve it a shell over that link. Driven from a web UI with a visual payload editor and a HIDScript engine.
honest_take: This is the clearest example in this batch of the trap the brief warns about: a beginner finds a 2019 tutorial, buys the wrong Pi, and gets a dead board. The project's last code push was October 2023, there are 210 open issues, and the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W support ticket (#307) has been open since October 2021 with the official image simply not booting. If you follow the README you must buy the original 32-bit Pi Zero W specifically. Technically the design is still excellent and the USB gadget tricks are the real thing - but you are adopting an abandoned Debian image, and the safer route today is Kali's own P4wnP1 A.L.O.A. build, which at least tracks a maintained distribution. Also worth knowing: it boots a full Linux system, so it is not instant - budget tens of seconds before the payload runs.

name: Digispark and CH552 BadUSB boards
firmware_note: There is no single project - you compile an Arduino sketch that types your payload. Converters such as Duckyspark translate existing DuckyScript into a sketch. The payload is baked into the firmware, so changing it means reflashing.

You get a bare board with a USB-A tongue and nothing else: no case, no storage, no wireless, no support.
skill_note: Cheap to buy, fiddly to use. On Digispark you fight the micronucleus bootloader, Windows driver installation via Zadig, and a plug-in timing window; on CH552 the flashing is easier but the toolchain is less familiar. Neither is a plug-and-play experience.
build_note: No soldering - buy the board, install the toolchain, compile a sketch with your payload, flash. The Digispark's micronucleus flow requires you to unplug the board, start the upload and then plug it in within a few seconds.
summary: The budget end of keystroke injection: two families of very cheap microcontroller boards with a USB-A plug on the PCB, flashed with a sketch that makes them enumerate as a keyboard and type a payload. The Digispark uses an ATtiny85 with software USB; CH552 boards use a WCH 8051 microcontroller with a real hardware USB peripheral. Together they are the standard answer to 'do I really need a $80 Rubber Ducky'.
honest_take: For most people, no, you do not need the expensive one - but know what you are giving up. There is no storage on either, so the payload is compiled into the firmware and changing it means reflashing, and there is no exfiltration path at all. And prefer CH552 over Digispark: the ATtiny85 bit-bangs USB in software (V-USB, low-speed only), which is why Digisparks are notorious for failing to enumerate on USB 3.x ports and hubs, for needing driver wrangling on Windows, and for the five-second bootloader delay before your payload runs. The CH552 has a hardware full-speed USB peripheral and roughly twice the flash for about the same money. Also note the ecosystem here is quiet: the big Digispark script collections were last touched in 2022-2023. Finally, if a seller markets one of these as a 'hacking device' at $25, you are paying $22 for a sticker.

name: DSTIKE Deauther Watch
firmware_note: Spacehuhn's ESP8266 Deauther, the firmware that made this whole product category exist. Ships pre-installed on DSTIKE hardware; the last tagged release is 2.6.1 from August 2021 and the long-promised v3 branch has never shipped.

The DIY equivalent is stark: the same firmware runs on a $3-4 NodeMCU or Wemos D1 Mini with no changes, so the $49 buys the watch strap, battery, OLED and case, not capability. Note DSTIKE also now sells an ESP32-C5 'Deauther32' line at $49-$169 which does reach 5GHz - but that runs DSTIKE's own firmware, not this one.
skill_note: Arrives flashed and working with an on-screen menu; the only real skill needed is understanding why it often does nothing, which is a networking question rather than a hardware one.
build_note: Ships assembled with firmware installed. Reflashing is a browser or Arduino IDE job over USB-C. The genuinely DIY route is to put the same .bin on any cheap ESP8266 board.
summary: A wrist-worn ESP8266 running Spacehuhn's Deauther firmware: it scans 2.4GHz networks and clients, then sends deauthentication and disassociation management frames to knock clients off, along with beacon spam and probe flooding. DSTIKE makes the hardware - a customised 4MB ESP-07 module, a 1.3in SH1106 OLED, a 1000mAh cell, a three-way switch and USB-C - and the firmware is the free open-source project everyone else uses too.
honest_take: Say this every single time: the deauth attack works only because 802.11 management frames were historically unauthenticated. 802.11w/PMF authenticates them, WPA3 makes PMF mandatory, and modern WPA2 gear increasingly turns it on - against any of those this watch does absolutely nothing, silently. It is also 2.4GHz only, so every 5GHz network is invisible to it. And it does not capture, crack or reveal anything: there is no handshake capture, no password recovery, nothing beyond disruption. On the firmware side, the last release was 2.6.1 in August 2021 and the last real code commit to the v2 branch was April 2022 - a v3 branch exists and has existed for years without shipping. The hardware is nice and the maker is legitimate; just understand you are paying $49 for a wearable case around a $4 board running frozen free software.

not_for: Any network with PMF enabled, which is all WPA3 - it will fail silently

firmware_note: The hat carries no processor of its own - it is a passive carrier board. All behaviour comes from Bruce, the ESP32 'predatory' firmware, running on the host display board. ESP32-DIV also publishes a CYD build that runs on the same host.

honest_take: First, answer the name directly: despite 'NerdMiner' in the branding, this IS a security tool, not a Bitcoin miner. The confusion is real and understandable - it is made by NMTech, the company behind the NerdMiner v2 solo-mining device, and marketplace listings routinely bundle the two in one title. The hat itself contains no miner and no processor at all; it is a passive carrier for radios that the host ESP32 drives. Second, the value case is strong: for around $30 all-in with no soldering you get most of what the ESP32-DIV asks you to build two custom PCBs for. What you give up is a maintained hardware design - it is an anonymous AliExpress board with no published schematic - and you inherit every limitation of the underlying radios: 2.4GHz only for Wi-Fi and BLE, fixed-code sub-GHz replay only, and PN532-class NFC that cannot recover MIFARE Classic keys.

firmware_note: Open source under CC-BY-4.0, served as a web panel from the device's own Wi-Fi. HTML and firmware assets live on the microSD, so the interface can be updated without reflashing.
vendor: April Brother (manufacturer); design by Joel Serna Moreno
price_note: $52.95-$64.95 at Rabbit-Labs depending on configuration (bare board, or bundled with a microSD and an acrylic or metal case), checked 2026-09-06. Also sold by April Brother on Tindie/AliExpress, SAPSAN Cybersec in Poland, KSEC in the UK (which offers a cheaper 'Lite' version) and Tienda Espia in Mexico. This is a vendor price. Building your own from an ESP32 board plus two CC1101 modules would cost about $20 in parts but you would be reimplementing a design whose gerbers are not published.
skill_note: Sold assembled and driven from a browser, but sub-GHz work itself demands you understand modulation, bit rate and frequency - the tool will happily let you transmit garbage.
build_note: Buy assembled; power it from USB or a battery, insert a microSD with the firmware and HTML assets, join its Wi-Fi and use the web panel. Firmware is open and reflashable.
summary: A sub-GHz research board: an ESP32 with two independent CC1101 transceivers and one nRF24L01, driven entirely from a web panel over its own Wi-Fi. The two CC1101s are the point - they can receive and transmit on different frequencies at the same time, which single-radio tools cannot do, and that opens up jamming-plus-capture and other two-frequency techniques. Captures can be exported for analysis in Universal Radio Hacker.
honest_take: The dual-CC1101 design is a genuine capability that a Flipper Zero does not have, and it is why this board still matters in 2026 - simultaneous transmit and receive on two different sub-GHz frequencies is what rolling-code capture-and-replay research actually requires. Two caveats. First, the board gives you the radio; it does not give you a working rollback attack - the separate ECRFv2-RollBack and Kaiju repos exist precisely because that is extra work, and those repos have not been touched since 2022-2023. Second, this is not really DIY: the hardware is manufactured by April Brother and the gerbers are not published, so despite the open CC-BY-4.0 firmware, you buy it. Maintenance is steady rather than energetic - last push October 2025, with the author's attention now largely on the Evil Crow Cable line.

legal.notes: Owning it is legal in most places. Transmitting on sub-GHz bands without a licence or outside permitted power and duty-cycle limits is an offence in most countries, and the dual-radio jamming techniques the hardware enables fall under the FCC's flat prohibition on jammer operation (47 U.S.C. 302a and 333). Opening a vehicle or garage you do not own is a separate and much more serious matter. MouseJack keystroke injection is unauthorised access. Check your local law; this is not legal advice.
